object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer account, the thing everything hangs off; created when a customer signs up.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off.

object_types.name: AccountNumber
object_types.definition: Six-digit sequential identifier for an account, never reused.

source_references.excerpt: Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: The agreement that an account pays a given amount on a given cycle for a given product, identified by subscription ID.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID.

object_types.name: SubscriptionId
object_types.definition: Unique generated identifier for a subscription, prefixed with SUB.

source_references.excerpt: Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: One of the three (soon four) products sold, identified by a product code.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.
Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: PricePlan
object_types.definition: The billing artefact that says what the customer pays and how often; generates the invoice line. Identified by a plan code.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.
CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: The feature bundle a customer gets -- seats, API access, SSO -- shown on the pricing page. Identified by name.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle

object_types.name: BundleName
object_types.definition: Unique name of a feature bundle.

source_references.excerpt: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me. ... Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: StartDate
object_types.definition: Date a subscription starts; always present.

source_references.excerpt: Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: EndDate
object_types.definition: Date a subscription ends; optional, present only for fixed-term or cancelled subscriptions.

source_references.excerpt: An open-ended subscription has no end date. ... A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: The billing cycle of a subscription: monthly or annual.

source_references.excerpt: Monthly or annual. ... Every subscription has exactly one billing period.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus
object_types.definition: Status of a subscription: trialing, active, past due, or cancelled.

source_references.excerpt: Trialing, active, past due, cancelled. ... Exactly one, yes.

object_types.name: PausedFlag
object_types.definition: A separate boolean indicating a subscription is paused; overlaps confusingly with status.

source_references.excerpt: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. ... it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs.

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of a change to a subscription's price plan, with its own identity, effective date, requester, and creation date.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. ... It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: ChangeId
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for a plan change record.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: EffectiveDate
object_types.definition: Date a plan change takes effect (distinct from the date it was made).

source_references.excerpt: we need to know who made it and when it takes effect, and those are different dates

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: The person who requested a plan change.

ambiguities.description: Two/three different concepts are all called 'plan': the price plan (billing artefact), the feature bundle (product's plan/tier), and the sales-negotiated deal. Only the first two are modeled here; the sales 'deal' concept is mentioned but explicitly deferred to another meeting. Should the sales deal concept also be captured in this model, and how does it relate to price plans?

source_references.excerpt: So we've got two things both called plan. ... the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated, which frequently matches neither.

ambiguities.description: MRR (Monthly Recurring Revenue) was explicitly identified as derived/computed from price plan and billing period, not stored. It has been deliberately excluded from the model as an attribute/fact type per the facilitator's decision. Confirm this exclusion is acceptable, or whether a derived rule/formula should still be documented in the model.

source_references.excerpt: It's worked out. It's the plan price normalised to a month. ... So it's derived from the price plan and the billing period. ... I'm not going to model it as an attribute of the subscription

ambiguities.description: The PausedFlag is a boolean that overlaps confusingly with SubscriptionStatus (e.g., a subscription can be 'active' and 'paused' simultaneously per the transcript). It's unclear whether PausedFlag should be integrated into status as a fifth value or truly kept as an independent orthogonal flag, and what constraints (if any) govern which statuses can be paused.

source_references.excerpt: There's also paused. ... Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. ... it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs. If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too.

ambiguities.description: The commercial/business rule for mid-term cancellation of annual subscriptions (run to term vs prorated refund vs credit) is explicitly undecided and parked. The model captures only the current system behavior (cancellation sets end date to paid-through date, no refund mechanism), but manual credits outside the subscription system have occurred. Should a 'Credit' or 'Refund' concept be modeled to capture these manual exceptions, pending the business decision?

source_references.excerpt: the four Tom's talking about were manual credits raised outside the subscription. ... What happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term ... is undecided.

ambiguities.description: The 'one active subscription per account per product' constraint is stated as an external uniqueness applying only to active subscriptions, but the underlying fact type 'Subscription is for Account with Product using PricePlan' does not itself carry an 'active' qualifier -- this constraint really applies only to a subset of subscriptions (those with status 'active' or possibly 'active-like', including trialing/paused). Clarify exactly which statuses count toward this uniqueness constraint (e.g., does trialing count? does paused count as active for this purpose?).

source_references.excerpt: One active subscription per account per product, enforced at the database level.

ambiguities.description: When an account closes and the same company returns, they are issued a new account number and treated as a new customer, losing historical continuity. This is a deliberate business/reporting decision but raises a granularity/identity question: should there be a separate 'Company' concept above 'Account' to track the real-world entity across account closures, distinct from the account identifier used for billing?

source_references.excerpt: If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting. ... Which drives me mad ... because it's the same company and we lose the history.

ambiguities.description: A fourth product is in discovery but not yet defined; the ProductCode value constraint of exactly {CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT} is stated as fixed 'today' only, meaning the value constraint may need to be revisited/loosened rather than treated as permanently closed.

source_references.excerpt: Fixed today. There's a fourth in discovery, but I'm not going to pretend I know what it is.

ambiguities.description: Whether the Subscription's denormalized 'current price plan' role (in fact type 'Subscription is for Account with Product using PricePlan') should be modeled as derived (from PlanChange history) or as an independently stored field is ambiguous -- Priya states it is a real stored field maintained by the change process, but Sam initially believed it was purely derived, and it was agreed the change history 'wins' in case of disagreement, implying possible data drift/bug scenarios. Clarify whether this should be modeled as a stored value with a subset/consistency constraint against PlanChange, or purely derived.

source_references.excerpt: The subscription's plan at any moment is derived. ... No, Sam, it does have a current plan field. ... And if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.
